name: Colin Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior setter on the big injection moulding presses at Halden Plastics, on the ring road estate. We make door panels and dashboard trims for two car makers. My shift starts at six, I walk the four presses, check the moulds are running clean, sort the scrap bins, and fix whatever the night shift left me. The best part is a tool change done in under forty minutes; the worst is standing over a 900-tonne press in August.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the part of the job only you can do, the bit people come to you for?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Reading a bad part. A door panel comes out with a sink mark or a short shot, and I can usually tell you if it's the barrel heat, the hold pressure or a blocked vent before anyone opens a screen. I'm also the union rep for our shift, so people come to me when the rota goes wrong. I've been there since I was nineteen, and I know those presses like my own kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's what I already think is happening. Everyone talks about AI, but on our floor the thing that changed things was a robot arm on Press 4, and that had nothing to do with chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. In the break room I'd tell the lads that the hype was the bosses' excuse to scare us into taking a flat pay deal. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be watching that robot arm on Press 4. Plateau or not, the company put it in last spring to take parts out of the mould, and it cost us one job on each shift. AI stalling doesn't stop them buying more arms like that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, keep the presses running and keep my head down. I'd push at the next union meeting for a written deal that any new robot comes with retraining, not redundancy. And I'd keep putting £150 a month away, because we're renting and Ines (my partner) wants a place of our own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, but not relaxed. The rent went up again in September, and the car makers keep cutting their orders. So even with AI going nowhere, I'm not sleeping on a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot arm cost one job on each shift. Who was that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marek, who'd been on the press for twelve years. He got moved to packing on less money, and he never says a word about it, but you can see it. That's the thing I'm watching for, more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your manager offered you a course on the new arm's controls, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. I'm good at what I do, and I don't want to spend my evenings learning to babysit the thing that pushed Marek out. Ines says I'm stubborn, and she's right.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was mostly a story bosses used to keep **pay deals** low.
I'd share the **union's take** online rather than post my own views.
think: The real threat on our floor is the **robot arm** on Press 4, not AI.
A stalled AI doesn't stop the company buying **more arms** that each cost a job.
do: Push the union for a **written deal** linking any new robot to retraining.
Keep saving **£150 a month** towards a place of our own.
Keep running the presses and **keep my head down**.
feel: **Relieved** that AI fizzled, but still uneasy about **rent** and falling car orders.
S0.quote: On our floor the thing that changed things was a robot arm on Press 4, and that had nothing to do with chatbots.
fieldNote: He separates AI from **robots** sharply; his fear is the arm already on the floor.
**Marek's demotion** to packing is the story that shapes everything he says.
He turns down training on the arm out of **loyalty and pride**, and admits it.

steps.text: Keep running the four presses on the same early shift
Table a motion asking for retraining before any new robot arm
Put £150 a month into the house deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. So the office lot get hit first, and we get hit slower. That sounds about how I'd expect it to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the planners and buyers upstairs should be worried before us. To friends I'd say this is where unions earn their money, because somebody has to make sure the savings don't all go to the shareholders. I'd sign any petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, slower isn't the same as never. Once the planning and ordering upstairs runs on software, it's easier for them to run the whole plant lights-out on nights, and that's my shift. I'd give it four or five years before they come for setters like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a jobs agreement with the company, in writing, before the next round of machines. I'd move our savings from three months up to five, and we'd skip the holiday in Portugal next summer. I wouldn't go near the AI stuff myself, but I'd ask the union to get someone who understands it to sit in on talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense. It's like watching the weather come in from across the field. You know it's coming, you just don't know if it's rain or hail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lights-out on nights. What does that mean on your floor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the presses with no one there, just robots unloading and a camera checking parts. Our plant manager went to a trade show in Germany and came back talking about lights-out nights like a holiday. That's when I started paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for someone who understands AI to sit in on talks, but you won't learn it yourself. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know what I'm good at. I can read a press and I can read a room full of angry blokes, and that's my job in those talks. Let someone else read the computer, as long as they're on our side.

say: I'd say the **planners and buyers** upstairs will feel this before the floor does.
I'd tell friends that **unions** must make sure savings don't all reach **shareholders**.
think: Software running planning makes **lights-out nights** easier, and nights are my shift.
I'd give it **four or five years** before setters like me are targeted.
do: Push for a written **jobs agreement** before the next round of machines.
Raise savings from three to **five months** by skipping the Portugal holiday.
Ask the union to bring in **an AI expert** for the talks.
feel: **Tense**, like watching a storm come in without knowing if it's **rain or hail**.
S1.quote: Our plant manager went to a trade show in Germany and came back talking about lights-out nights like a holiday. That's when I started paying attention.
fieldNote: He reads Steady Disruption through the **night shift**, where he expects robots to land first.
He delegates the technology to others and keeps **organising** as his own role.
His savings move is real: the **Portugal holiday** goes first.

steps.text: Push for a written jobs agreement before new machines arrive
Skip next summer's Portugal holiday to reach five months saved
Cut takeaways and the second streaming service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before my thirtieth. And robots three years after that, so 2031, when I'm thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why you need strong unions and a government that taxes the companies doing it. I'd be loud about it, on the picket line if there was one. I'd tell people not to blame the person next to them on the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking side of my job is small. I don't plan, I don't order, I set and fix. So 2028 hits the office, and I've got till about 2031 before an arm can change a mould better than me. Three years sounds long, but on a car parts contract it's two model cycles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get savings up to six months and stop paying into the house fund, because a deposit means nothing if I've got no wage. I'd get the union to fight for a redundancy deal now, while they still need us to train the robots. And I'd talk to Ines about her care home, because people will still need looking after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. Angry too, because I did everything right. I learned the trade, I'm the best setter on the site, and it still might not matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're not buying a flat, not yet. She'd be gutted, she's been looking at places on Mill Road. Then I'd probably say her job's safer than mine, which would feel strange to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you won't learn the new machines. In this picture, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If it's that or the dole, I'd learn to set up the robot cell. But I'd want the company to pay for it and do it in work hours. I'm not giving them my weekends to train my own replacement.

say: I'd say this is why we need **strong unions** and taxes on the companies doing it.
I'd tell people not to blame **the person** working next to them on the line.
think: My job is mostly hands-on, so I'd have until about **2031** before arms replace me.
**Three years** is only two model cycles on a car parts contract.
do: Pause the house fund and build savings to **six months**.
Push the union for a **redundancy deal** while the company needs us to train robots.
Talk with Ines about leaning on her **care home** wage.
feel: **Sick and angry**, because being the best setter on site might not matter.
S2.quote: I learned the trade, I'm the best setter on the site, and it still might not matter.
fieldNote: He calculates his runway in **car model cycles**, not years.
Even this resistant man would retrain, but only **on company time**.
The flat on **Mill Road** is the first thing he'd give up.

steps.text: Stop paying into the flat deposit and build six months saved
Push the union for a redundancy deal before the robots arrive
Ask to learn the robot cell setup on paid work hours
Plan to lean on Ines's care home wage if laid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. That's a bit more breathing room, but it's still my early thirties gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one: unions, tax the robots, protect people. But with five years, I'd say it louder to the politicians, because there's time for them to actually do something. I'd go knock on doors for whoever promised a real plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, eight years until a robot does my job is enough time to get out ahead of it, but I don't really know where to go. Everything I'm good at is hands-on. If it's all robots by 2034, the hands-on stuff is exactly what goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd campaign for a jobs guarantee and get stuck in with the union. I'd save hard, maybe get to six months by 2028. And I'd probably look at maintenance on the robot cells, because someone's got to fix them, even if I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and a bit lost. I feel like I've been told the bridge I'm on closes in eight years and nobody's built the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and the people who sold them the robots. Not the robots, they're just tools. And the government, if they sat on their hands for five years knowing it was coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does robot maintenance actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grease, sensors, gripper fingers, calibration. I'd need a course at the college on the industrial estate, probably two nights a week for a year. I'd hate every minute of the theory, but I'd get through it.

say: I'd demand **unions, a robot tax** and protection for workers.
I'd **knock on doors** for a party with a real jobs plan.
think: Everything I'm good at is **hands-on**, which is exactly what robots take by **2034**.
There's time to get ahead of it, but I **don't know where** to go.
do: Campaign for a **jobs guarantee** with the union.
Sign up for a **robot maintenance** course at the local college.
feel: **Uneasy and lost**, like the bridge closes in eight years with no replacement.
S3.quote: I feel like I've been told the bridge I'm on closes in eight years and nobody's built the next one.
fieldNote: More time turns him from defence to **politics**: door-knocking and campaigning.
He blames **owners and government**, never the machines themselves.
He'd retrain into robot **maintenance**, reluctantly, and says so.

steps.text: Knock on doors for a party promising a jobs guarantee
Push the union for a staged plan to protect setters
Take the college robot maintenance course two nights a week
Save towards six months of expenses by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years to prepare. That's a different story, because I'd be thirty-seven and could still change trades properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the chance to get it right. Use the ten years to retrain people with proper funding, not some app on your phone. I'd say it at union meetings and to anyone at the pub who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be nervous. Ten years is long enough to change, but I don't like change, and I know I'd put it off. Ines would have to give me a kick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and buy the flat on Mill Road, because a decade is enough to pay a good chunk off. I'd stay in the union and push for the company to fund courses. Around 2030 I'd probably start an electrical course, because wiring is hands-on and there'll be a lot of robots needing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. It feels like I'd have a fair shot, if I actually use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ines would have to give you a kick. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd sit me down with a printout of the college courses and a pen. She did the same when I wouldn't go to the dentist for a year. She knows I'll do it once it's written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the robots still come for the electrical work by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably some of it, yeah. But somebody has to wire the factories they work in. Maybe I'm kidding myself, but I'd rather be wiring the robots than standing next to one.

say: I'd call for **properly funded retraining**, not a phone app.
I'd say this decade is **the chance** to get it right.
think: Ten years is long enough, but I know I'd **put it off**.
My partner Ines would have to **push me** to start.
do: Buy the **Mill Road flat** and pay down a good chunk.
feel: **Worried but steadier**, with a fair shot if I use the time.
S4.quote: Maybe I'm kidding myself, but I'd rather be wiring the robots than standing next to one.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him make **life plans**: the flat comes back.
He knows his own habit of **putting things off**, and names his partner as the push.
His plan B is **electrical work**, still hands-on, which he half-doubts.

steps.text: Buy the Mill Road flat with the saved deposit
Push the union for company-funded courses for setters
Start an evening electrical course at the college around 2030

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years for the office, five for me, and nobody ready. What would help is a law that says a company can't bring in a robot without a deal with the union, and proper money for retraining in work hours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people without a union. I've got one, but half the plants on our estate don't have a union. If it goes fast, they're the ones who just get a letter on a Friday.

headlineQuote: Half the plants on our estate don't have a union. If it goes fast, they're the ones who just get a letter on a Friday.
portrait: Colin is a 27-year-old **senior setter** at a plastics plant making car door panels and trims.
He is the shift's **union rep** and judges every change by what happened to his colleague Marek.
He never uses AI and resists learning the **robot arm**, out of pride and loyalty.
His fear grows with speed: **uneasy** in a plateau, **alarmed** when AGI arrives fast.
With ten years he would buy a flat and retrain as an **electrician**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the office goes in two years and his presses about three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a **union deal** before any robot is installed.
**Paid retraining** in work hours, not in the evenings.
